goals: Estimate spatially-distributed recharge across the Naches watershed
Quantify recharge spatial variability and its drivers (soil, topographic position)
Provide indirect validation against water-table depth observations where available
key_processes: Infiltration and percolation through the soil column
Snowmelt contribution to recharge (timing and magnitude)
drivers_to_resolve: topographic position (elevation as spatial coordinate, not climate driver)

model_choice.rationale: ELM single-column runs stratified across soil and elevation bands provide spatially-distributed recharge estimates (via QDRAI). This is a site-based spatial sampling campaign with indirect validation against WTD observations.

answerable: Spatial pattern of recharge across the watershed given uniform forcing
Soil texture control on recharge (via infiltration, percolation, ET)
Topographic position effect on recharge (as a spatial coordinate—valley vs ridge)
Indirect validation of recharge estimates against water-table depth observations

not_answerable.aspect: Elevation control on recharge via climate gradients (orographic precipitation, temperature lapse)
not_answerable.why: Framework uses uniform forcing across all columns—cannot represent elevation-driven precipitation/temperature gradients that dominate mountain recharge patterns
not_answerable.needs: Elevation-downscaled meteorological forcing (PRISM or similar) to vary precip/temp with elevation

not_answerable.why: No recharge measurements exist in the domain (observations_missing)
not_answerable.needs: In-situ recharge measurements (lysimeters, tracer studies, or water-balance closure at gauged sub-basins)

not_answerable.aspect: Lateral groundwater redistribution effects on recharge
not_answerable.why: ELM is 1-D column model—QDRAI is vertical drainage only, does not account for lateral flow convergence/divergence
not_answerable.needs: 3-D subsurface flow model (PFLOTRAN) or coupled ELM-PFLOTRAN to represent lateral redistribution

not_answerable.aspect: Confirmation of uniform 500 mm/yr recharge claim
not_answerable.why: Claim contradicts physical expectation for heterogeneous mountain watershed; no observations to validate against; framework cannot test the climate-driven variability that would refute/support it

sampling_strategy.approach: Stratified spatial sampling across elevation bands and soil classes
sampling_strategy.n_justification: 3 elevation bands × 3 soil classes × 2 replicates per stratum = 18 exploratory columns. This resolves the factorial design (elevation position × soil) with light replication to assess within-stratum variability. Replication is minimal because the question is about spatial pattern, not uncertainty quantification.
sampling_strategy.placement_logic: Within each elevation band, sample across the soil gradient. Concentrate columns in mid-elevation (rain-snow transition, 800-1400 m) where recharge processes are most dynamic (snowmelt timing, mixed precip phase). In low elevation, sample valley bottoms and alluvial fans (high recharge potential). In high elevation, sample ridges and slopes (snow accumulation zones). Avoid steep slopes >30° where ELM's 1-D assumption breaks down most severely.
sampling_strategy.replication: 2 columns per stratum (elevation × soil combination) to capture within-stratum spatial variability and provide a basic uncertainty estimate on stratum-mean recharge.

sampling_plan.reason: Valley floor alluvial fans—high infiltration, rain-dominated, expected high recharge
Valley floor moderate soils—baseline recharge for rain-dominated zone
Valley floor low-permeability soils—tests infiltration limitation on recharge
Rain-snow transition, high infiltration—captures snowmelt recharge pulse in permeable substrate
Rain-snow transition, moderate soils—most representative of watershed, critical for spatial average
Rain-snow transition, low permeability—tests whether snowmelt overwhelms infiltration capacity
Snow-dominated ridges, high infiltration—maximum snowmelt recharge potential
Snow-dominated slopes, moderate soils—typical high-elevation recharge
Snow-dominated, low permeability—tests whether frozen/saturated soils limit recharge

validation_design.comparison: analog — long-term mean simulated recharge (QDRAI) compared to steady-state water-table depth via conceptual water-balance relationship (high recharge → shallow WTD in unconfined aquifers). Not direct co-location because ELM does not simulate water table.
validation_design.metric: Spearman rank correlation between simulated recharge and observed WTD (inverse relationship expected: high recharge areas should have shallower water tables, assuming similar aquifer properties)
validation_design.n_validation_points: unknown — depends on USGS well density in Naches HUC, likely 5-15 wells

validation_design.observation_source: Fan et al. 2013 gridded WTD prior (1 km resolution)
validation_design.comparison: aggregated — spatially-averaged simulated recharge compared to spatial pattern of Fan WTD across the watershed. Tests whether high-recharge zones (simulated) align with shallow-WTD zones (observed).
validation_design.metric: Spatial correlation (Pearson r) between gridded recharge estimates (interpolated from column locations) and Fan WTD grid
validation_design.n_validation_points: ~200 grid cells covering Naches HUC at 1 km resolution

experiment_summary.primary_treatment: Baseline forcing (1980-2018 climatology, uniform across domain), native soil properties from gridded soil dataset, default ELM vegetation (PFT from land-cover data)

requires_capabilities.why: To represent orographic precipitation gradients and temperature lapse rates that drive elevation-dependent recharge patterns in mountain watersheds
requires_capabilities.blocks: Testing elevation as a climate driver (currently elevation is only a spatial coordinate; columns at different elevations receive identical forcing)

requires_capabilities.capability: Gridded soil property dataset for Naches HUC
requires_capabilities.why: To assign realistic soil texture, hydraulic conductivity, and porosity to each column based on its location
requires_capabilities.blocks: Soil stratification (currently assumes soil classes exist but does not specify data source)

requires_capabilities.why: To place columns at representative elevations within each elevation band (low/mid/high) by sampling the actual DEM
requires_capabilities.blocks: Deterministic placement of columns in elevation strata

requires_capabilities.why: To constrain column placement within the Naches HUC-8 watershed boundary

requires_capabilities.capability: USGS well data ingest and spatial query
requires_capabilities.why: To identify well locations within Naches HUC and extract observed water-table depths for validation

requires_capabilities.capability: Fan et al. 2013 WTD dataset ingest and spatial extraction
requires_capabilities.why: To extract gridded WTD values for the Naches domain for spatial validation
QDRAI is the recharge proxy—must be in the output variable list and post-processed to annual totals
requires_capabilities.blocks: Recharge estimation (if QDRAI is not output, the experiment cannot proceed)

requires_capabilities.capability: Spatial interpolation tool for recharge estimates
requires_capabilities.why: To create a continuous recharge surface from the 18 point estimates for comparison with gridded Fan WTD
ELM soil moisture and snow states must equilibrate before recharge estimates are meaningful (likely 10-20 year spin-up)
requires_capabilities.blocks: Physically realistic recharge estimates (without spin-up, initial conditions dominate)

requires_capabilities.capability: Direct recharge measurements (lysimeters, tracers, or gauged sub-basin water balance)
requires_capabilities.why: To validate simulated recharge directly rather than via the indirect WTD proxy
requires_capabilities.blocks: Direct validation of recharge estimates (currently only indirect validation is possible)

requires_capabilities.capability: 3-D subsurface flow model (PFLOTRAN) or ELM-PFLOTRAN coupling
requires_capabilities.why: To represent lateral groundwater flow and test whether 1-D recharge estimates (ELM QDRAI) are biased by neglecting lateral redistribution
requires_capabilities.blocks: Accounting for lateral flow effects on recharge (ELM assumes purely vertical drainage)

assumptions: Uniform forcing across the domain is acceptable for isolating soil effects, but severely limits elevation-driven recharge variability
ELM QDRAI (sub-surface drainage) is a reasonable proxy for recharge in the absence of lateral flow representation
Water-table depth observations provide an indirect constraint on long-term recharge via steady-state water balance (high recharge → shallow WTD in unconfined systems)
Soil property data exist and can be spatially queried to assign realistic hydraulic parameters to each column
The 1980-2018 forcing period is long enough to estimate climatological mean recharge (transient trends are not the focus)
Replication factor of 2 per stratum is sufficient for basic within-stratum variability assessment
The user's claim of uniform 500 mm/yr recharge is a hypothesis to be tested, not a constraint on the design
open_questions: What is the source and spatial resolution of the soil property dataset for Naches? Does it include hydraulic conductivity and porosity, or only texture class?
How many USGS wells exist within the Naches HUC, and what is their temporal coverage (are they suitable for long-term mean WTD)?
What is the published source for the 500 mm/yr uniform recharge claim? Does it provide spatial detail or uncertainty bounds?
Is there a preferred time period within 1980-2018 for the forcing (e.g., exclude drought years, or use the full climatology)?
Should the design include a sensitivity test on forcing period (e.g., wet vs dry years) to assess recharge variability, or focus only on long-term mean?
Are there any gauged sub-basins within Naches where streamflow data could provide an independent water-balance constraint on recharge?
